claim: By the German Mittelstand definition, size is not the gate: firms with 500+ employees or >EUR 50m turnover still count as Mittelstand if up to two individuals/their family hold >=50% and sit in management (unity of ownership and control). So a 1,000-5,000 employee owner-managed firm is 'Mittelstand', not 'SME'.
quote: Zugleich zaehlen aber auch Unternehmen mit 500 und mehr Beschaeftigten oder mehr als 50 Mio. Euro Jahresumsatz zum Mittelstand/Familienunternehmen, wenn sie die oben genannten Kriterien erfuellen.

claim: Under the EU statistical definition a medium enterprise has fewer than 250 employees and turnover <= EUR 50m; 250+ employees is a large enterprise. A 1,000-5,000 employee firm is therefore a LARGE enterprise by EU rules even when it is 'Mittelstand' by German framing.
publisher: European Union (EU SME definition, Rec. 2003/361/EC; per UNESCWA/EU sources)
source_title: Small and medium-sized enterprises - EU definition
quote: the turnover of medium-sized enterprises (50-249 employees) should not exceed EUR 50 million

claim: In SMEs there is typically no global mobility program, no experts and no dedicated team; the move is owned by HR/generalists and handled case-by-case with individually negotiated, often over-generous terms.
source_title: Global mobility management strategies for small- and medium-sized companies
quote: how can SME proceed when they don't have any global mobility programs, experts, or dedicated team members available to manage the move?

claim: SMEs facing this typically bring in an external resource to coordinate the process, ensure compliance and manage the external providers - i.e. they outsource rather than build an internal function.
vendor_used_today: outside coordinator / RMC or consultant appointed ad hoc
source_title: Global mobility management strategies for small- and medium-sized companies
quote: companies usually appoint an outside resource to help coordinate all the required processes, ensure adequate compliance and manage external providers.

claim: The core compliance/knowledge requirements do not scale down with company size - the same legal, tax and duty-of-care knowledge is needed whether moving 10 or 100 employees. Implication: the 'knows things you don't' pain exists across the range, but volume differs.
move_volume: 10 to 100 employees (illustrative range cited by Mercer)
source_title: Global mobility management strategies for small- and medium-sized companies
quote: It doesn't matter whether the company is moving 10 or 100 employees - relying on detailed global HR knowledge, an understanding of legal requirements, managing employees' expectations, and providing the right level of support are required, and these requirements don't change with the size of the company.

claim: As the number of assignees grows, costs and complexity rise and ad-hoc generous packages stop being justifiable; process gaps, inefficiencies and compliance issues (e.g. social-security overruns) surface. This is the point at which structured tooling becomes valuable - it is a volume-triggered need, not a size-triggered one.
source_title: Global mobility management strategies for small- and medium-sized companies
quote: As the number of assignees grows, the costs and complexities increase, and over-generous individual packages can no longer be justified by business reasons.

claim: Ownership of mobility is split by company profile: some organisations have a dedicated global mobility function, others hand it to HR or another department. The 'HR owns it' pattern is explicitly a real, common alternative - not universal.
who_owns_mobility: dedicated GM function OR HR/other department
publisher: Santa Fe Relocation (John Rason) via Relocate Magazine
source_title: The evolving role of global mobility: from back office to strategic business partner
quote: In some organisations there is a dedicated global mobility function, while in others it is handled by Human Resources (HR) or other departments.

claim: Larger organisations can fund mobility technology; smaller companies are less likely to. Budget/tech-adoption capacity rises with size - relevant to willingness to pay for a tool vs. absorbing the work in HR.
budget_owner: larger orgs fund tech; smaller orgs constrained
publisher: Santa Fe Relocation (John Rason) via Relocate Magazine
source_title: The evolving role of global mobility: from back office to strategic business partner
quote: while big business might have the budget to implement new systems, smaller companies are less likely to do so.

claim: At larger firms mobility is a small specialist team carrying a large assignee load (e.g. five people for ~300 international workers), and many still run programs on spreadsheets. Signals: at scale a dedicated specialist owns it (weakening 'knows things you don't'), yet the tooling gap persists.
publisher: Santa Fe Relocation (John Rason) via Relocate Magazine
source_title: The evolving role of global mobility: from back office to strategic business partner
quote: you might end up with a team of five people in mobility who used to look after 300 international workers

claim: The main industry benchmark of global mobility programs is drawn from 456 MULTINATIONAL enterprises across 29 jurisdictions and 12 industries - i.e. the companies studied are large enough to have identifiable 'mobility leaders'. SME/HR-generalist buyers are structurally under-represented in the canonical benchmark data.
quote: Based on insights from 456 multinational enterprises across 29 jurisdictions and 12 industries, this year's report uncovers six imperatives shaping the future of global mobility.

claim: Even among large benchmarked programs, 72% of mobility teams struggle with analytics scalability and most rely on spreadsheets rather than advanced tools - confirming an unmet structured-tooling need even where a dedicated function exists.
quote: Seventy-two percent of mobility teams struggle with analytics scalability; most rely on spreadsheets over advanced analytics tools.

claim: The incumbent vendor category SMEs/mid-market default to is Relocation Management Companies (RMCs) - Graebel, SIRVA, Cartus, Santa Fe - a multi-billion-dollar corporate relocation services market projected to reach ~USD 28.6bn by 2031 (6.7% CAGR). These are the incumbents a mid-market ICP would already be under contract with.

claim: Compliance exposure is triggered by a single person in a new jurisdiction (permanent-establishment / tax risk), not by move volume - which is exactly the 'invisible requirement' fear ReloPass targets and which exists even at low-volume SMEs.
publisher: Santa Fe Relocation (John Rason) via Relocate Magazine
source_title: The evolving role of global mobility: from back office to strategic business partner
quote: Even one person working in a different jurisdiction can leave an organisation vulnerable to being taxable in that country if the remote work duties trigger a permanent establishment risk.
